title: Spanish adolescents and fake news: level of awareness and credibility of information (Los adolescentes españoles frente a las fake news: nivel de conciencia y credibilidad de la información)
screen_reason: Cross-sectional survey of 480 randomly sampled Spanish secondary students (Seville, May-June 2019) with the ad hoc CHECK-M questionnaire. One item asks whether they have seen news online or on social media that they thought was 'fake news', and the results report a share of respondents at the affirmative end ('more than 90% of the subjects say that they ... have seen fake news and thought it was fake'), which qualifies as a RECALL exposure share. The study's aim is media literacy, but a descriptive share is reported, so §1's 'aim is something else' clause applies.

estimates.platform: Self-report survey about news seen online or on social media
estimates.date: May and June of the 2018-19 academic year
estimates.measure_type: % of adolescents who say they have seen news online or on social media that they thought was 'fake news'
estimates.value_raw: 'more than 90% of the subjects say that they have heard of fake news, that they have seen fake news and thought it was fake and that they are aware that there is information that is deliberately designed to trick citizens'; Figure 1 labels only two segments for this item, 27% and 62% (the 'Most likely' and 'Yes, for sure' ends of the 1-5 scale); item mean 4.44 (SD 0.902) on the 1-5 scale
estimates.denominator: 480 students aged 14-18 (mean 16) in the third and fourth years of compulsory secondary education and the first two years of baccalaureate, province of Seville, Spain; simple random sample of a target population of 74,026 enrolled students (95% confidence, 4.46% confidence interval)
estimates.definition: Respondent endorsing the CHECK-M item 'You've seen news online or in the social media and thought it was "fake news"' towards the affirmative end of a 1-5 Likert scale (1 = 'No, never', 5 = 'Yes, for sure'); the reported share is the authors' summary of the response frequencies for the three awareness items taken together
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given to respondents; the questionnaire's own gloss is that "'fake news' is deliberately invented/written to trick people", and the literature review describes fake news as content 'fabricated with the intention of hiding the truth, distracting, changing reality or deliberately using lies to influence consumers' behaviour'
estimates.source_quote: These data are reinforced with an analysis of the response frequencies, which shows that more than 90% of the subjects say that they have heard of fake news, that they have seen fake news and thought it was fake and that they are aware that there is information that is deliberately designed to trick citizens (Figure 1).
estimates.page_loc: Results (first objective), p. 9; Table 1 (Scale 1 item means); Figure 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondents' own judgement of what counts as fake news; no external verification. Ad hoc 'CHECK-M' questionnaire built from Blakeslee's CRAAP test and the Ofcom (2017/2018) parent items, reworded for direct student response and pilot-tested for cognitive validity; Scale 1 (knowledge and awareness of fake news) Cronbach's alpha = 0.655 with 59.4% total variance explained. Administered on paper in schools with a researcher present.
estimates.moderator_quote: The target population of the study was comprised of the 74,026 students enrolled in the third and fourth years of compulsory secondary education and the first and second years of baccalaureate in the province of Seville (Spain) ... To choose them, we did a simple random sampling for finite samples assuming a confidence level of 95%, a confidence interval of 4.46% and a precision level of 50%. The final sample was comprised of a total of 480 students (N = 480) between the ages of 14 and 18
estimates.notes: value_kind=range_not_point because the paper never prints a per-item percentage: the only share statement is the prose 'more than 90%', asserted jointly for all three Scale-1 items, and the two labelled Figure 1 segments for THIS item (27% + 62%) would have to be added to produce 89% - a cross-category sum that R8 forbids, and one that in fact contradicts the '>90%' claim for this item. The segment labels are also unlabelled in the figure text, so the mapping to 'Most likely' and 'Yes, for sure' is inferred from the legend order. borderline=true accordingly. If the review needs a point value, the defensible verbatim single-category candidate is 62% answering the top category ('Yes, for sure'), but that mapping is an inference from the figure and I did not treat it as verbatim. denom_scope=population per the survey rule. Population is adolescents aged 14-18 in one Spanish province, so not a general adult population.

missed_or_uncertain: Deliberately NOT extracted: (a) the other two Scale-1 items, 'You've heard about fake news' (mean 4.52; Figure 1 segments 20% and 70%) and 'You're aware that fake news is deliberately invented/written to trick people' (mean 4.74; segments 12% and 83%). Both measure AWARENESS OF THE CONCEPT rather than encountering misinformation, which §1 does not cover (only self-reported encounter/exposure or sharing counts). (b) Every item of Scale 2, 'What do you do if you see fake news on the Internet?' (I tell a friend 3.80, I tell my parents 3.10, I share it and say it's not true 2.63, I leave a comment 2.34, I report it on social media 2.11, I tell a teacher 1.76, with Figure 2 category percentages and the prose 'more than 75% ... would tell a friend', 'approximately 50% ... parents', '75% ... would not tell their teacher', 'around 70% of the subjects who would not report it or are not sure', '70% of the respondents would say nothing'). These are HYPOTHETICAL reactions to encountering fake news, explicitly excluded as sharing intentions rather than observed sharing; the 'I share it and say it's not true' item is in any case a corrective-sharing intention. (c) The entire credibility scale (Table 2, five CRAAP factors) - Likert means only, no share of respondents, so no row per the instructions. (d) Tables 3 and 4 (t-tests/ANOVA of credibility by gender, school year and awareness level) - test statistics, no shares. (e) All literature-review figures, which are quoted from other studies and barred by R8: 31% of 10-18s had shared a story later found false (Robb 2017), 77% of 15-24s in the Eurobarometer, UK awareness 73% (2017) to 78% (2018) (Ofcom), 82% (Wineburg et al.), 34%/13%/42% (Notley et al., Australia), 2% and 49.9% (National Literacy Trust), 47.2% to 76.2% (NewsWise evaluation), 8 in 10 and 43% (Ofcom 2018), 7% and 11% (Loos et al.), 93%/25%/19% (Skuola.net, Italy), 58%/30%/12% (Greek Safer Internet Center), 10%/60%/86%/71%/62%/45%/30%/19%/68% (Austrian and Swedish studies).

rob.design: Non-experimental cross-sectional survey (ex post facto). Frame: simple random sampling for finite populations from the 74,026 students enrolled in the last two years of compulsory secondary education and the first two of baccalaureate in the province of Seville, Spain; final n = 480 aged 14-18 (mean 16, SD 1.885), 51% male, 99% owning a mobile phone; 95% confidence, stated confidence interval 4.46%. No response rate, no non-response analysis, no weighting, and no information on how many schools were approached or refused. Instrument: ad hoc 'CHECK-M' questionnaire (three sections; the first, on device habits, is not reported), 1-5 Likert scales, pilot-tested for comprehension; Scale 1 alpha = 0.655 (weak), Scale 2 alpha = 0.757, credibility scale alpha = 0.879 with AVE/CR reported per factor. Paper administration in schools with a researcher present (possible social-desirability and demand effects on self-assessed skill). Exposure is measured purely by self-report with no verification, and the results report means plus a single prose percentage rather than an item-level frequency table, so the exposure share cannot be recovered exactly. Analysis: descriptive frequencies, t-tests and ANOVA in SPSS v24.
